summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented for Córdoba. A trans visitor here stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America, and is assessed against the national position on lethal violence rather than against any local deviation.

Nationally nothing about being trans is criminalised. Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition: since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government-issued identification is changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That legal position does not contain the violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and even after the president ordered an urgent investigation no one had been arrested as of 14 April 2025. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." Thirteen trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025. The pattern a visitor should expect nationally is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested.

Some of the targeting is territorial and organised. In Caquetá department armed groups have run a "social cleansing" campaign, distributing flyers on the street and via WhatsApp that name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023. Discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to premises and to detention are governed by court order and decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Protection machinery exists without having closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising.
tangentialFactors:
Antioquia and Caquetá are cited as illustrations of a national pattern, not as proxies for Córdoba. Reporting on both rests on the same finding: armed actors and unarrested daylight assaults operate where the state's protection is thin, and the Millerey case shows that a presidential order for investigation does not by itself produce an arrest.

The count of 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025 sits against 41 killings in 2023 and 8 between February and April 2024, so annual totals across the three years are not drawn from comparable reporting periods and should not be read as a trend line.

Caquetá's flyer campaigns and forced displacements are described in the sources as continuing after the Millerey case, in reporting that ties them to the country's decades-long civil conflict rather than to a discrete episode.
localsOnly:
Residents of Córdoba rely on the national identification regime: since June 2015 a notarised document suffices to change the sex marker, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 removes any surgical requirement. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree and the May 2018 executive decree impose the procedural obligations under which local institutions in education, health care and prisons operate.

Local residents who marry abroad are covered by the National Registry memo requiring notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside Colombia, with the attendant visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights.

Local employment conditions mirror the national finding that discrimination confines trans women largely to hairdressing or sex work, and residents face the same organised-threat environment documented elsewhere in the country where armed groups circulate named kill lists.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Córdoba-specific source is present in the inventory, so departmental police practice, hate-crime charging outcomes, local facilities access and the operation of the 2016 and 2018 decrees in Córdoba's own institutions remain unsourced rather than established.

The number of arrests in the Millerey case after 14 April 2025 is not sourced here; the inventory records only the position as of that date.

National kill counts for 2023, 2024 and 2025 come from different reporting windows, so any comparison of years is unresolved on the available material.
